Steel.description: A strong iron-based alloy used in buildings, vehicles, tools and packaging. Recycled content and the furnace route change its impact.
Steel.tradeoff: Steel is energy- and carbon-intensive to make, but it can be recycled repeatedly without losing strength, which makes long service life and recovery especially valuable.
tips: Ask for recycled content and the production route used.
Design parts to be separated from coatings and plastics.
Size sections to avoid using more steel than needed.

Aluminium.description: A light, corrosion-resistant metal used in cans, window frames, vehicles and electronics. Primary production is very electricity-intensive.
Aluminium.tradeoff: Primary aluminium scores poorly on carbon and energy, yet recycled aluminium needs only a fraction of that energy, so recycled content matters more than almost anything else.
tips: Specify a high share of recycled aluminium.
Ask about the electricity source used for smelting.
Keep alloys and coatings simple to ease recycling.

Concrete.description: A mix of cement, water, sand and aggregate used for foundations, floors and structures. Cement is the main source of its impact.
Concrete.tradeoff: Concrete is durable and locally made, but cement production releases a lot of carbon, and crushed concrete is usually downcycled rather than reused as concrete.
tips: Ask for mixes with lower cement content or cement replacements.
Avoid over-specifying strength and thickness.
Plan for reuse of elements, not just demolition.

Glass.texture: radial-gradient(circle at 30% 28%, rgba(255,255,255,.38), transparent 40%), radial-gradient(circle at 72% 72%, rgba(255,255,255,.18), transparent 35%), linear-gradient(135deg, #3f9a7c, #1f6b55 55%, #2f8a6c)
Glass.description: A transparent material made by melting sand, soda ash and limestone. Used for windows, bottles, jars and screens.
Glass.tradeoff: Glass needs high melting temperatures, but container glass recycles well when it is collected by colour and kept free of contamination.
tips: Prefer reusable containers over single-use ones.
Avoid mixing glass with ceramics or bonded films.
Check that local collection accepts the glass type.

Plastic (PET).description: A clear, light fossil-based polymer used mainly for drinks bottles, food trays and polyester fibre.
Plastic (PET).tradeoff: PET is light to transport and is one of the more widely collected plastics, but it depends on fossil feedstock and recycled quality falls with colour, labels and contamination.
tips: Use clear, unpigmented PET with easily removed labels.
Ask for recycled PET (rPET) content.
Prefer refillable formats where the product allows.

Paper / Cardboard.description: Wood or plant fibres formed into sheets and board, used for printing, boxes and protective packaging.
Paper / Cardboard.tradeoff: Paper and cardboard have low carbon and energy scores and recycle well, but fibres shorten with each cycle and coatings, grease or moisture can stop them being recovered.
tips: Look for recycled or certified fibre sources.
Avoid plastic coatings and laminated finishes.
Right-size packaging and keep it dry and clean.

Leather.description: Tanned animal hide used for shoes, bags, furniture and car interiors. Farming and tanning drive most of its impact.
Leather.tradeoff: Leather can last for decades with care, but its upstream impact is high and tanned leather is very difficult to recycle.
tips: Ask how the leather was tanned and where it came from.
Choose products designed to be repaired.
Keep products in use for as long as possible.

Copper.description: A highly conductive metal used in wiring, pipes, motors and electronics. Mining and refining ore is energy-intensive.
Copper.tradeoff: Copper has a heavy production footprint but keeps its value and properties when recycled, so recovery from cables and devices is key.
tips: Ask for recycled copper where performance allows.
Make wiring and coils easy to remove at end of life.
Avoid bonding copper to other materials.

Brick.description: Fired clay blocks used for walls, paving and facades. Kiln firing is the main source of energy use.
Brick.tradeoff: Bricks are very durable and can be reclaimed, but cement mortar often makes clean separation and reuse difficult.
tips: Consider reclaimed bricks where available.
Use lime mortar to allow future reuse.
Source locally to limit transport of heavy units.

Rubber.description: An elastic material from natural latex or synthetic polymers, used for tyres, seals, flooring and footwear.
Rubber.tradeoff: Rubber is long-lasting, but vulcanised rubber cannot be melted down again, so it is mostly ground into crumb or burned for energy.
tips: Check whether the rubber is natural or synthetic.
Choose replaceable seals and soles over bonded ones.
Look for products using recycled crumb rubber.

Cotton fabric.texture: repeating-linear-gradient(0deg, rgba(120,100,70,.16) 0 1px, transparent 1px 3px), repeating-linear-gradient(90deg, rgba(120,100,70,.16) 0 1px, transparent 1px 3px), linear-gradient(#ddd2bf, #cdc1ab)
Cotton fabric.description: A natural plant fibre woven into clothing, towels and furnishings. Growing it can require a lot of water and agrochemicals.
Cotton fabric.tradeoff: Cotton is renewable and biodegradable, but water use is high and blended fabrics are hard to recycle back into new fibre.
tips: Look for organic or responsibly grown cotton.
Avoid blends if fibre-to-fibre recycling matters.
Wash cooler and less often to extend garment life.

Polyester fabric.description: A synthetic, fossil-based fibre used in clothing, upholstery and outdoor gear. Durable, quick-drying and inexpensive.
Polyester fabric.tradeoff: Polyester is durable but fossil-based, sheds microfibres when washed, and is rarely recycled back into textiles.
tips: Prefer recycled polyester where available.
Avoid blends with natural fibres.
Choose durable items you will keep for longer.

PVC.description: Polyvinyl chloride, a rigid or flexible plastic used for pipes, window frames, flooring and cables.
PVC.tradeoff: PVC is long-lasting in buildings, but additives and chlorine content make recycling and safe disposal more complicated.
tips: Check for alternatives in pipes, flooring and packaging.
Ask about additives such as plasticisers.
Use take-back schemes for offcuts and old products.

Wood.description: A versatile natural material used in structures, interiors and everyday products. Species, sourcing and finishes change its impact.
Wood.tradeoff: Wood has lower carbon and energy scores, but recovery is not guaranteed. Coatings, adhesives and local collection can limit recycling.
tips: Check species, origin and responsible sourcing.
Design for repair, reuse and disassembly.
Confirm local recovery options for treated wood.

Clay.description: A natural earth material shaped into pottery, tiles and plasters. Unfired clay can return to the ground; fired clay becomes ceramic.
Clay.tradeoff: Raw clay is abundant and needs little processing, but firing adds energy and fired ceramics cannot easily be turned back into clay.
tips: Consider unfired clay plasters for interiors.
Source locally to reduce transport.
Choose durable glazes to extend product life.
